## Answer: $2n-4$ (not fully verified)

I did not derive this rigorously or check it against the literature, so treat it as a plausible answer rather than a proof.

**Lower bound (a non-HIST graph with $2n-4$ edges).** Take $K_{2,n-2}$ with parts $\{a,b\}$ and $\{x_1,\dots,x_{n-2}\}$. Each $x_i$ has degree 2 in $G$, so in any spanning tree $T$ it must be a leaf, since degree 2 is forbidden. Then $a$ and $b$ cannot be joined in $T$: any $a$–$b$ path would pass through some $x_i$ as an interior vertex, giving it degree 2. So $K_{2,n-2}$ has no HIST and has $2(n-2)=2n-4$ edges.

**Why adding one edge fails.** Adding $ab$ gives $K_2+\overline{K}_{n-2}$, which has a HIST: the star centred at $a$ spans everything, with all other vertices as leaves. Adding an edge $x_1x_2$ instead also yields a HIST: let $x_1$ be adjacent to $a$, $b$ and the leaf $x_2$, and let all other $x_i$ be leaves of $a$. Here $x_1$ has degree 3 and every other vertex has degree 1 or $a$ has large degree. I checked these cases by hand but did not exhaust all $(2n-3)$-edge 2-connected graphs.

**Upper bound.** I did not prove that every 2-connected graph of order $n\ge 13$ with $2n-3$ or more edges has a HIST. The threshold $n\ge 13$ suggests a competing family with roughly $n+c$ edges for some constant $c$, but I did not identify one.

ANSWER: $2n-4$
